turns.prompt_text: Where is the best place to purchase ten feet of wood cost-effectively in Iowa? I am building a car ramp
turns.response_html:
For a heavy-duty, load-bearing project like a car ramp, finding the right balance of cost-efficiency, strength, and length is critical. Since car ramps require high structural integrity to safely hold thousands of pounds, standard framing lumber (like SPF) or pressure-treated lumber rated for ground contact are your best bets.

Here are the most cost-effective options in Central Iowa to source 10-foot or longer dimensional lumber, along with tips for your ramp build:

1. High-Volume Big Box Retailers (Best for Out-of-the-Box Pricing)

For standard 10-foot or 12-foot lengths of dimensional lumber (like 2x8s, 2x10s, or 2x12s), big-box stores typically offer the lowest consumer-level prices and high stock availability.

  • Lowe’s (Ames): Located right on Airport Road, this is an incredibly convenient spot if you need to quickly browse the bunks for straight, knot-free boards. They consistently stock 10-foot and 12-foot pressure-treated and construction-grade framing lumber.
  • The Home Depot (Ankeny): Located off SE Delaware Ave, they feature an excellent selection of structural lumber and heavy-duty fasteners (like structural timber screws). Their Pro Desk area makes it easy to pull a vehicle up for quick loading of longer stock.
  • Menards (Ankeny / Des Moines area): If you are willing to drive slightly south of Ames or work out of the Ankeny area, Menards often edges out competitors slightly on raw price per board foot for dimensional lumber, especially if you catch their rolling 11% rebate windows. Their drive-in lumber yard format makes sorting through heavy 2x10s or 2x12s straightforward.

2. Local Independent Lumber Yards (Best for Material Quality)

If you are looking for higher-grade wood with fewer twists, crowns, or massive structural knots (which can compromise a car ramp), regional yards are an excellent choice. Their bulk structural prices are often highly competitive with big box stores.

  • Munn Lumber / Mead Lumber (Ames & Ankeny locations): Munn has deep roots in central Iowa, with yards on Airport Road in Ames and NE 69th Place in Ankeny. They carry robust structural framing lumber, engineered wood, and heavy treated stock. Because they primarily service contractors, their dimensional lumber is often stored better and straighter than what sits on the shelves of big retailers.

Material & Cost-Efficiency Tips for a Car Ramp

  • Settle on 12-Foot Stock Over 10-Foot if Needed: Depending on the specific width or thickness you choose (such as 2x10s or 2x12s), 10-foot boards can occasionally be a specialty cut with lower inventory. Check the price-per-foot on 12-foot boards—sometimes they are highly commoditized and priced so closely to 10-foot boards that buying the 12-footer and trimming it down gives you better yield or extra material for structural blocking/cleats.
  • Prioritize Wood Grade Over Lowest Price: For a car ramp, completely avoid economy or "stud" grade wood. Look for #2 Grade or better (Standard & Better). Ensure there are no large knots running through the center or edges of the board where the tires will exert maximum flexing pressure.
  • Consider Moisture/Treatment: If these ramps will be used outdoors, on a garage floor prone to dampness, or stored on dirt/gravel, opt for Pressure-Treated (PT) lumber rated for Ground Contact. If they are strictly for indoor dry garage use, standard kiln-dried Douglas Fir or Southern Yellow Pine (SYP) will save you money and weigh significantly less, but they must be kept dry to prevent rotting and structural failure over time.
  • Don't Skimp on Fasteners: Budget a few extra dollars for high-quality construction adhesive (like PL Premium) and structural timber screws (like GRK or Spax) rather than standard drywall or wood screws. Mechanical fasteners combined with heavy wood glue will prevent the ramp layers from shearing under the intense shifting weight of a vehicle.

Depending on local inventory updates, 12-foot boards can sometimes have a lower cost-per-foot than 10-foot boards. turns.prompt_text: How many 10-foot or 12-foot 2x12 boards do I need to build a standard solid-stacked car ramp, and what are the cut lengths?
turns.response_html:
To build a solid-stacked car ramp out of 2x12 dimensional lumber, buying 12-foot boards is actually the most efficient path.

The standard, highly reliable design uses a 4-layer pyramid stack with a tire stop at the back end. This gives you a total lift of 6 inches (since a 2x12 actually measures $1.5 \text{ inches} \times 11.25 \text{ inches}$), which is the sweet spot for basic oil changes and under-car maintenance without creating an aggressively steep incline that scrapes low bumpers.

Here is the exact layout, material count, and cut list to build a pair of ramps.

Total Materials Needed

  • Boards: Two 2" x 12" x 12' boards.
  • Screws: One box (approx. 50 count) of 2.5-inch or 3-inch heavy-duty wood or structural deck screws (avoid drywall screws, as they can shear under pressure).
  • Adhesive: One tube of heavy-duty construction adhesive (like Loctite PL Premium or Gorilla Construction Adhesive).

The Cut List (Per 12-Foot Board)

You will use one 12-foot board per ramp. This ensures zero wasted lumber and keeps your build mathematically perfectly balanced. Make the following straight crosscuts on each of your two boards:

  • Layer 1 (Base): 48 inches (4 feet)
  • Layer 2: 38 inches
  • Layer 3: 28 inches
  • Layer 4 (Top Platform): 18 inches
  • Tire Stop: 5 inches (cut from the remaining 7-inch scrap piece)

💡 Beveling Option: If your car sits incredibly low to the ground, you can use a circular saw to cut a 45-degree angle on the leading approach edge of Layers 2, 3, and 4. If you have a standard truck or SUV, standard straight crosscuts form small "steps" that tires can easily climb without beveling.

Assembly Steps

Safety & Storage Note

Once assembled, let the construction adhesive cure fully for 24 hours before driving a vehicle onto them. The glue creates a unified block of solid wood, transferring the load straight to the ground. Store these in a dry area of your garage to prevent moisture from warping the wood or degrading the adhesive bonds over time.

turns.prompt_text: Because I cannot fit 12 ft boards into my car, I'm likely going to have to cut them where I purchased them. The easiest way would be to cut them in half, but is this feasible?
turns.response_html:
Yes, cutting them completely in half into 6-foot sections at the store is 100% feasible, and it will still give you a rock-solid ramp design with zero wasted lumber.

Most home improvement stores (like Lowe's or Menards) have a radical arm saw or a panel saw station in the lumber aisle, and associates will gladly make a few quick crosscuts so you can load the wood into a standard car or SUV.

By cutting your two 12-foot boards directly in half, you will end up with four 6-foot boards. Here is how to adjust your cut layout for that exact setup:

Revised Cut List (Using Four 6-Foot Pieces)

To build a pair of ramps, you will assign two 6-foot boards per ramp. Since they are already cut to 72 inches, your cuts at home become incredibly simple:

Ramp 1 (Requires Board A and Board B)

  • From Board A (72"): Cut one 48" piece (Layer 1 Base). This leaves you with a 24" scrap piece.
  • From Board B (72"): Cut one 38" piece (Layer 2) and one 28" piece (Layer 3). This leaves you with a 6" piece (perfect for your Safety Tire Stop).
  • The Remainder: Take the 24" scrap piece from Board A, and trim it down to 18" to create your Layer 4 Top Platform.

Ramp 2 (Requires Board C and Board D)

  • Repeat the exact same cuts using your remaining two 6-foot boards.

What You End Up With (Per Ramp)

Your final dimensions remain completely unchanged from the original heavy-duty design, meaning you lose zero structural integrity:

Ramp LayerTarget LengthSource
Layer 1 (Base)48 inchesCut from Board A
Layer 238 inchesCut from Board B
Layer 328 inchesCut from Board B
Layer 4 (Top)18 inchesTrimmed from Board A's leftover piece
Safety Tire Stop6 inchesBoard B's exact leftover piece

Pro-Tips for Getting Wood Cut at the Store

  • Account for the "Kerf" (Saw Blade Thickness): Saw blades eat up about $1/8 \text{ inch}$ of wood per cut. Because Board B requires two cuts (72" total minus 38" and 28"), your remaining piece will be slightly under 6 inches (around $5\ \textstyle\frac{7}{8}\ \text{inches}$). This is absolutely fine—it is still plenty wide to serve as your safety tire stop.
  • Ask Nicely: If the store isn't incredibly busy, the associate might even let you make your specific project cuts right there on their radial saw, saving you from having to break out the saw at home at all. If they have a policy against complex cut lists, just ask them to "chop the 12-footers dead in half," and you'll be out the door in minutes.

turns.prompt_text: How many ramps does this get me? Two or four?
turns.response_html:
This gets you two ramps (one complete pair) — exactly what you need for one axle (either both front tires or both rear tires).

Here is the quick math on how those four 6-foot boards are used:

  • Boards A & B combine to make Ramp #1 (Driver's side)
  • Boards C & D combine to make Ramp #2 (Passenger's side)

If you ever need a full set of four ramps to lift the entire vehicle simultaneously (front and back), you would just double the order and buy four 12-foot boards total, cutting each in half at the store to leave with eight 6-foot pieces.
